concept.name: Zero-coupon rate
concept.definition: The yield earned on an investment that makes a single payment at maturity with no intermediate coupons, for a specific maturity. It is the building block of the spot (zero-coupon) curve used to discount individual future cash flows.
concept.intuition: It is the pure interest rate for money delivered at one exact future date, with nothing paid in between — like the rate on a Treasury bill or a STRIP.
concept.mechanics: For a zero-coupon instrument the rate follows directly from price and face value; for coupon-bearing markets the zero-coupon rates are bootstrapped from bond prices so all input securities price without error. The U.S. Treasury notes its published par yield curve is a semiannual bond-equivalent curve and that it does not publish daily zero-coupon curve rates.
concept.formula: z_t = (F / P)^(1/t) − 1, where P is the price today, F the single payment at maturity, and t the time in years.
concept.failure_modes: Zero-coupon rates are model-derived rather than directly quoted for most maturities, so they inherit bootstrapping and interpolation assumptions; liquidity differences between coupon bonds and STRIPS can also create small inconsistencies.
concept.misconceptions: The zero-coupon rate for maturity t is not the yield of the t-year coupon bond; confusing par yields with spot rates produces systematic valuation errors when the curve is sloped.
concept.example: A 2-year zero-coupon bond priced at 92.10 per 100 face implies a 2-year zero rate of (100/92.10)^(1/2) − 1 ≈ 4.2%.

citations.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Interest Rates — Frequently Asked Questions
